## Task 1 - Slate Health Check {#sec-task-1}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

target_cols <- c("title", "budget", "roi", "franchise_status", "primary_genre", "release_year", "cast_size", "primary_company")
task_1_data <- data |>
  filter(
    budget >= 1000, # filtering out movies with a recorded budget below 1000 USD
    budget < 550000000, # most expensive movie ever was Jurassic World Dominion with a budget of 549 million so let's cut anything higher for being fake
    revenue >= 1000,
    release_year >= 1974 # the franchise tag is not used until 1974, despite franchise films such as James Bond existing before then
  ) |> 
  dplyr::select(all_of(target_cols)) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) na_if(x, 0))) |> 
  mutate(
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status)
  )
```

This is a high-level overview of the financial health and composition of the studios historical slate.

Some cleaning has been done to prepare the data for this report. Some films in the dataset had missing or unrealistically low values for budget or revenue. Most dollar amounts in the dataset have been entered as the whole figure, but in some cases it appears they have been recorded as hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars. For example, *Escape from Tomorrow* has a recorded budget of 650 in the dataset. The film's actual reported budget was $650,000.

Given the large initial size of the dataset (no. of films = `r nrow(data)`) we decided to filter out any films with budget or revenue amounts less than 1000 to cut films with missing or implausible values. We also removed any films with a reported budget higher than 550 million USD (the largest budget ever reported for a film). The franchise tag is not used for any film pre-1974 even when films *were* part of a franchise (like James Bond); given the importance of comparison between Original and Franchise films to this report we have also filtered for only films released in 1974 or later.

This left us with `r (nrow(task_1_data))` films to analyse, of which franchise films made up `r 100*(task_1_data |> filter(franchise_status == "Franchise") |> nrow())/nrow(task_1_data)`% of the films in our cleaned dataset, vs the `r 100*(data |> filter(franchise_status == "Franchise") |> nrow())/nrow(data)`% they made up in the original dataset. We are happy that this does not represent a large enough change in the composition of our data to skew our analysis. 

### Summary of data

::: {#nte-franchise-coding .callout-note title = "Coding for Original vs Franchise"}
\fontsize{6}{8}\selectfont

First films in a franchise are labelled as "Original" rather than as part of a franchise, and are therefore included in the data for the "Original" variable (see @tbl-slate-overall-summary, where *Paranormal Activity* is an Original film, and *Paranormal Activity 2* is a Franchise film.)

Additionally, some films that are clearly part of a franchise are not labelled as such; i.e. all 4 Pirates of the Caribbean movies are labelled as Original movies.

As such, the figures in @tbl-slate-overall-summary should be taken as *indicative* of overall trends only, not treated as absolute truths.

:::


```{r}
#| label: tbl-slate-overall-summary
#| tbl-cap: Summary statistics for the historical slate

# this entire table was the bane of my existence
# i hate rendering tables to PDF
# Did you know that if you try to use a linebreak like \n in gt or \\\\ in kable, rendering to PDF will cause that new line to appear in a new cell in column 1?
# instead of being sensible and remaining in the same cell?
# so here's a nasty workaround creating variable names that are all unique permutations of whitespace to create the rows I want

task_1_data |> 
  group_by(franchise_status) |> 
  summarise(
    `Number of movies` = as.character(n()),
    `Most Common Genre` = paste0(
      names(which.max(table(primary_genre))),
      " (n = ",
      max(table(primary_genre)),
      ")"
    ),
    `Mean Production Budget (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(mean(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Median Production Budget (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(median(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Production Budget Standard Deviation (USD millions)` = as.character(
      round(sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)
    ),
    `Mean Return on Investment (ROI)` = as.character(
      round(mean(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    `Median ROI` = as.character(
      round(median(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    `ROI Standard Deviation` = as.character(
      round(sd(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
    ),
    `Max Production Budget (USD millions)` = as.character(round(max(budget, na.rm = TRUE) / 1e6, 2)),
    ` ` = paste0("*(", title[which.max(budget)], ")*"), 
    `Minimum Production Budget (USD)` = format(min(budget, na.rm = TRUE), big.mark = ","),
    `  ` = paste0("*(", title[which.min(budget)], ")*"), # unique amounts of whitespace so that each of these variables have "different" names and the table prints correctly
    `Best ROI` = as.character(round(max(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)),
    `   ` = paste0("*(", title[which.max(roi)], ")*"),
    `Worst ROI` = as.character(round(min(roi, na.rm = TRUE), 2)),
    `    ` = paste0("*(", title[which.min(roi)], ")*"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 

  # pivoting long and then wide to get Franchise and Original to be our variable names
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -franchise_status,
    names_to = "Statistic",
    values_to = "Value"
  ) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = franchise_status,
    values_from = Value
  ) |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_markdown() |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "left",
    columns = Statistic
  ) |> 
  cols_align(
    align = "center",
    columns = c(Original, Franchise)
  ) |> 
   # manually setting column widths because on top of everything else, LuaLaTeX has failed me here as well
  cols_width( 
    Statistic ~ "2.3in",
    Franchise ~ "2.2in",
    Original ~ "2.3in" # googling says these values should add up to 6.8in to fit in a PDF correctly
  ) |>
  tab_options(
    table.font.size = px(9)
  ) |>
  # changing the rows with a Statistic value that only has whitespace (i.e. the film title rows) to have a smaller font size 
  tab_style(
  style = cell_text(size = px(8)),
  locations = cells_body(
    columns = c(Original, Franchise),
    rows = grepl("^\\s+$", Statistic) 
    )
  )
```

### Slate composition over time

We wanted to look at how the composition of the historical slate by genre has changed over time, with a specific focus on the genres Meridian is interested in.

Worth noting is that although we have some data from 2015 on, it is not complete data and is therefore not included in @fig-genre-line-chart as it skews visual temporal analysis. It is unclear if the data we have from 2014 is fully complete, but it has been included until we are given a compelling reason to exclude it.

```{r}

#| fig-cap: Line charts showing changing composition of slate over time; film release dates have been aggregated into 5 year blocks to make trends more visible
#| layout-ncol: 2

genre_counts <- task_1_data |> 
  filter(
```

### Summary

From the plots in this section, and given what we know about how films are coded (@nte-franchise-coding), we can draw some conclusions already.

Sequels are generally more expensive to make than original films, and are generally a safer bet than original films; they have a higher ROI on average, and are less likely to fall below an ROI of 1 (meaning they generally at least make their money back) (@tbl-slate-overall-summary and @fig-genre-plots). However, original films have much higher variability in ROI and may represent a riskier but more lucrative investment strategy.

The three genres that have consistently seen the most films released over the last 25+ years are Action, Comedy and Drama films (@fig-genre-line-chart-1), all of which Meridian is invested in. 

There was a significant spike in the relative amount of Franchise films being released around 1990, which then completely flattened out prior to 2000 (@fig-status-area-chart-2). With the recent trend towards a higher percentage of releases being Franchise movies, we should look towards that period in the 90s when developing our strategy for the next decade. This will be discussed more in @sec-task-2.

## Task 2 {#sec-task-2}

Budget data are often skewed, and the median is often more meaningful than the mean when describing a budget for typical franchise and original categories. 
Here I will be using bootstraping to find 95% interval estimate for the difference in median budget between the two groups. As bootstraping simulates repeated samples from a population like the csv provided here, it can help us to describe the uncertainity in the data.

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic-boxplots
#| fig-cap: Boxplots showing distribution of budgets and Return on Investment (Revenue divided by Budget) for Original vs Franchise films
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-subcap: 
#| - Budget
#| - ROI; dashed red line is at ROI = 1 i.e. films above the line made a profit, films below lost money

task_1_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = franchise_status, y = budget/1e6, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Film Status",
    y = "Film budget (USD millions)"
  ) 

task_1_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = franchise_status, y = roi, fill = franchise_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    trans = transform_pseudo_log(), # using a function from the scales package to compress the y axis, as we have some extreme outliers in Original movies for ROI
    breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000, 20000)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Film Status",
    y = "Return on Investment\n(Revenue/Budget)"
  )
```

The @fig-basic-boxplots-1 shows differnce in median of sequals and originals using a boxplot. The median budget of franchise is higher than the original (The data analysed here is from 1974 and later as discussed in @sec-task-1) which raises the concern of the leadership about the budget. However in @fig-basic-boxplots-2, the difference between ROI's of both the categories shows a much needed aspect to increase the overall profits of the production house.  

```{r}
clean_data_t2 <- data |>
  dplyr::select(franchise_status,budget) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) na_if(x, 0))) |> 
  mutate(
    franchise_status = factor(franchise_status)
  ) |> 
  filter(!is.na(franchise_status), !is.na(budget))


t2_sum_table <- clean_data_t2 |> 
  group_by(franchise_status) |> 
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    median = median(budget, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(budget, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

```{r}
point_est_t2 <- t2_sum_table$median[t2_sum_table$franchise_status == "Franchise"] - t2_sum_table$median[t2_sum_table$franchise_status == "Original"]
```

As interpreted from the @fig-basic-boxplots and the @tbl-slate-overall-summary, the 'original' franchise status have the lower median which shows that the production budgets are biased towards the 'franchise' category as the median ROI in not much in case of originals. To confirm this we will use bootstraping method that takes n number of samples, here 5000 from the dataset with repeated values as TRUE so that it can include random observations multiple times. The reason of this bootstrapping is to confirm the baised selection of budget allocation by the leadership. The point estimate of the data is `r point_est_t2` which we will use to confirm if bootstarped estimate is similar or not. If yes, then the budget allocation is truely are leaned towards 'franchise' category. 

```{r}

perform_bootstrap <- function() {
  
  one_boot <- clean_data_t2 |> 
    group_by(franchise_status) |> 
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE)
  
  one_result <- one_boot |> 
    summarise(med_budget = median(budget), .groups = "drop") |> 
    summarise(
      diff_median = med_budget[franchise_status == "Franchise"] - 
                    med_budget[franchise_status == "Original"]
    )
  
  return(one_result)
}

set.seed(36)

bootstrap_results <- map_dfr(
  .x = 1:5000,
  .f = ~ perform_bootstrap()
)

ci_95 <- quantile(bootstrap_results$diff_median, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

The percentile bootstrap confidence interval of the data is `r ci_95[1]` and `r ci_95[2]`. The interval suggests that the population median difference is plausible between these values based on the data and bootstrap method.

### Does it verify leadership concern?

```{r}
bootstrap_results |>  
  mutate(diff_median = diff_median/1e6) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_median)) +
  geom_histogram(color = "white", bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = point_est_t2/1e6, color = "red", linewidth = 0.7)+
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_95[1]/1e6, linetype = "dashed")+
  geom_vline(xintercept = ci_95[2]/1e6, linetype = "dashed")+
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distribution: Difference in Median Budgets",
    subtitle = "Franchise Median - Original Median (Simple line = observed, Dashed = 95% CI)",
    x = "Difference in Median Budget (Millions USD)",
    y = "Frequency"
  )
```

This shows that the median difference is well above zero and similar to the point estimate which supports the concerns of the leadership of franchise slate absorbing much larger budgets than original slate.
   
Additionally from @sec-task-2 @fig-basic-boxplots-2, we can interpret that the originals have higher number of outliers that drastically increases the profits of the production houses but overall originals have a lower median ROI. 

### Summary

The median is the best way to summarise the budget data as they are always right skewed and using mean won't provide any acceptable information. We needed to know about the difference in median of the two facets of franchise status to confirm the concern of the leadership about the baised budget allocation towards franchises. By boostraping the median difference of the `franchise_status` categories and creating a histogram of it showed that the median difference is well above zero (near 18 Million) which confirms the concern about budget allocations prioritisation. 

However, as stated in @sec-task-1, the sequels are much expensive to make than the originals and they have higher ROI than the originals, due to this reason the production houses are more inclined towards producing sequals as they have much better chance of creating profits than the originals. But from @sec-task-2 @fig-basic-boxplots-2, we can interpret that the originals have higher number of outliers that drastically increases the profits of the production houses. However, the median ROI in origianls is low hence producing originals seems risky.

### Advice
The advice to the leadership is to focus on original movies that have high potential such as the genre that have the most profitable originals with lower risk such as horror for 2017 and gradually increase the budget allocation for them while comparing the profits generated by both categories simultaniously and changing or refining the new original story selection strategy and finding a optimised allocation stratergy that maximises the profits for the company. 

According to @sec-task-1, @fig-genre-plots-4 shows the ROI of originals in Meridian's focus genre where less than 1 shows the movie was a flop or a disaster. The genre horror comes up at the top with second lowest flop rate and really high potential for a big profit.

Choosing more originals from horror genre in the slots for 2017 releases carefully and strategically, provides more room for higher profits and gradually trying and testing with different genre, creating an optimal budget allocation for movies can increase the profits with a high margin. 

## Task 3 {#sec-task-3}
### Part 1: Production Budget Modelling
With the goal to construct a model that models an appropriate movie budget distribution, a competitor budget analysis was conducted as a credible reference point in line with industry standards. This was performed by sampling the budgeting model from Universal Pictures Studios, which is a direct industry competitor, and fitting a realistic probability model for Meridian to follow after similar data processing from previous analysis. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#Check distribution
universal <- task_1_data |> 
  filter(primary_company == "Universal Pictures") |> 
  mutate(budget = budget/1e6  )

ggplot(universal, aes(x = budget,)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10)+
  labs(title = "Distribution of Universal Pictures Film Budgets")

```

After data processing, the budget distribution is right skewed and only contain positive values. Therefore, exponential, Gamma, Log normal and  Weibull distribution can be selected for model evaluation. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
#Fit plot
budget_normal <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "normal"
)


budget_exp <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "exponential"
)

budget_gamma <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "gamma"
)

budget_weibull <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "weibull"
)

budget_lognormal <- fitdistr(
  universal$budget,
  densfun = "lognormal"
)

```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
#qqplot
qq_normal <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_normal$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_normal$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Normal")

qq_exponential <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qexp,
    dparams = as.list(budget_exp$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qexp,
    dparams = as.list(budget_exp$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Exponential")

qq_gamma <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qgamma,
    dparams = as.list(budget_gamma$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qgamma,
    dparams = as.list(budget_gamma$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Gamma")

qq_weibull <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qweibull,
    dparams = as.list(budget_weibull$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qweibull,
    dparams = as.list(budget_weibull$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Weibull")

qq_lognormal <- 
  ggplot(universal, aes(sample = budget)) +
  stat_qq(
    distribution = qlnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_lognormal$estimate)
  ) +
  stat_qq_line(
    distribution = qlnorm,
    dparams = as.list(budget_lognormal$estimate)
  ) +
  labs(title = "Log-normal")

qq_normal+ qq_exponential + qq_gamma + qq_weibull + qq_lognormal
```

The qq plot indicates normal and log normal are the worst fits as tails deviate the most from the reference line. The Exponential and Gamma model have the best fist as the right tail have the smallest distance from the reference line and most of the points overlap with the line.

```{r}
#fit AIC
AIC(
  budget_normal, 
  budget_exp, 
  budget_gamma, 
  budget_weibull,
  budget_lognormal
) |> 
  rownames_to_column(var = "model") |> 
  arrange(AIC) |> 
  gt()
```

The Gamma model has lowest AIC, which paired with the fitting of the qqplot, which suggests that it is the best at fitting budget data. However, the Weibull model would also be sufficient as the AIC is slighly larger than the gamma distribution by 1. 

###  Part 2: Downside Risk Analysis for Action Movie ROI

Action movies have been established as capital-intensive to produce, which can be proved as risky for budget investment in order to yield significant revenue. As a result, risk analysis into the bottom performing 25% movie ROI was performed across the entire film industry to model conservative target ROI to aim for, 

```{r}
action_roi <- task_1_data |> 
  filter(primary_genre == "Action", !is.na(roi)) |> 
  pull(roi) 

#observed ROI at 25% percentile
observed_q <- quantile(action_roi, 0.25) |> 
  round(3)

```
The observed 25% percentile of Action Movie ROI was `r observed_q`
```{r}
#Bootstrap Test
set.seed(5242)

bootstrap_results <- tibble(
  replicate = 1:1000
) |>
  mutate(
    boot_q = map_dbl(replicate, function(i) {
      action_boot <- sample(
        x = action_roi,
        size = length(action_roi),
        replace = TRUE
      )

      quantile(action_boot, probs = 0.25)
    })
  )

bootstrap_ci <- bootstrap_results |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(boot_q, probs = 0.025),
    upper = quantile(boot_q, probs = 0.975)
  )

#Method 2: SE multiplier
t_multiplier <- qt(0.975, df = length(action_roi) - 1)

bootstrap_se_ci <- bootstrap_results |>
  summarise(
    boot_se = sd(boot_q),
    lower = observed_q - t_multiplier * boot_se,
    upper = observed_q + t_multiplier * boot_se
  )

#Make into table
tibble(
  Calculation_method = c("Percentile bootstrap", "Bootstrap SE (t)"),
  Lower_Bound = c(
    bootstrap_ci$lower,
    bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  ),
  Upper_bound = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper
  )
) |> 
  gt()
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-align: center

#plot bootstrap
q3plot1 <- ggplot(bootstrap_results, aes(x = boot_q)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.025) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_q,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(bootstrap_ci$lower, bootstrap_ci$upper),
    linewidth = 1
  )+
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrap in 25% quantiles",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples",
    title = "Bootstrap distribution using Percentile Method",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

q3plot2 <- ggplot(bootstrap_results, aes(x = boot_q)) +
  geom_histogram(boundary = 0, binwidth = 0.025) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = observed_q,
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = c(bootstrap_se_ci$lower, bootstrap_se_ci$upper),
    linewidth = 1
  )+
  labs(
    x = "Bootstrap in 25% quantiles",
    y = "Number of bootstrap samples",
    title = "Bootstrap distribution using Standard Error Method",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the observed difference"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
q3plot1
q3plot2

```

```{r}
check <- tibble(
  method = c("Percentile bootstrap", "Bootstrap SE (t)"),
  gap_below = c(
    observed_q - bootstrap_ci$lower,
    observed_q - bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  ),
  gap_above = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper - observed_q,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper - observed_q
  ),
  width = c(
    bootstrap_ci$upper- bootstrap_ci$lower,
    bootstrap_se_ci$upper- bootstrap_se_ci$lower
  )
)

check |>  gt()
```

Both methods to calculate the confidence interval use the bootstrapped sample, which assumes the sample of Action films is representative of the population. Overall, both the percentile interval and the standard error interval equal to (0.76, 1.00). 

The percentile method does not consider symmetry as it takes the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles directly from the bootstrapped distribution, while the bootstrapped standard error method assumes the distribution is symmetric and approximately bell-shaped which places the lower and upper bounds equidistant from the observed 25th percentile (0.89). Both methods yielded identical intervals due to the bootstrapped distribution appearing to be approximately symmetric around the observed estimate with little skewness. This indicates the symmetry assumption is upheld where the standard error interval relies on this assumption holding as true. Although either method is suitable here, the percentile method is generally preferred because it does not depend on the symmetry assumption.

### Summary

Based on the analysis, it is recommended to select the Gamma distribution for the simulation. It had the best fit for the budget data as it matched the QQ-plot reference line the closest and had the lowest AIC value after evaluating five different models. It captured the right skew in budgets where few movie budgets had more expensive budgets compared to the majority of movies. 

In this sample, 25% of action films had an ROI of 0.576 or lower. We are 95% confident the true 25th percentile of the ROI for all action films across all studios lies between 0.463 and 0.679. For a conservative risk figure to plan around, Finance should consider 0.463 (46.3% return) for an underperforming Action film. 

## Task 4 {#sec-task-4}

```{r}

task4_data <- task_1_data |> 
mutate(
    flop = case_when(roi < 1 ~ "Flop",
                    TRUE ~ "Not flop"),
    flop = factor(flop, levels = c("Not flop", "Flop"))
  )
glimpse(task4_data)
```

The new flop variable only has two possible outcomes, which means it can be modeled by a Bernoulli distribution, where the parameter p measures the probability that a move is a flop. Hence, logistic regression is the appropriate choice as the log function $\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$ ensures the predicted probabilities remain between 0 and 1. The linear regression is not suitable as it assumes outcomes are continuous and normally distributed, while the flop variable only takes 0 and 1. Poisson regression is also not suitable as it is used when the outcome is a count with no upper limit. 

```{r}
task4_data <- task4_data |> 
  filter(!is.na(cast_size), primary_genre %in% meridian_genres ) |> 
  mutate(log_budget = log(budget)) |>
  mutate(across(c(log_budget, cast_size),
                ~ (.x - mean(.x)) / sd(.x),
                .names = "{.col}.z"))

freq_logistic_model <- glm(
  formula = flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget.z + cast_size.z,
  family = binomial,
  data = task4_data
)
summary(freq_logistic_model)
```
Using the 5% significant level, franchise status, cast size, and the Animation, Comedy and Horror genres are significantly associated with the probability of a film flopping. The Drama genre and Log budget are not significantly associate with the odds of a movie flopping due to the p values being greater after adjusting for other predictors. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
confint(freq_logistic_model)

exp(coef(freq_logistic_model))
exp(confint(freq_logistic_model))

```
```{r}
#| fig.width: 12
#| fig.height: 12
check_model(freq_logistic_model)
```


The frequentist model reproduces the observed numbers of flops and non-flops. All VIFs are close to 1, which suggests no evidence of collinearity. Most binned residuals fall within the error bounds with a few bins around 20–30% fall below the lower bound of predicted probabilities, suggesting the model slightly overestimates the probability of a flop in this range. The homogeneity of variance and normality plots are not relevant for a binary outcome. We also assume the films are independent and that each numeric predictor has a linear relationship with the log-odds of a flop.
### Bayesian REgression Model

```{r}
library(brms)
bayes_logistic <- brm(
  flop ~ primary_genre + franchise_status + log_budget.z + cast_size.z,
  data = task4_data,
  family = bernoulli(),
  prior = c(
    prior(normal(0, 2), class = Intercept),
    prior(normal(0, 1), class = b)
  )
)

```
```{r}
summary(bayes_logistic)
plot(bayes_logistic)
```
```{r}
pp_check(bayes_logistic)
```
